claim: Genomic imprinting refers to the mono-allelic and parent-specific expression of a subset of genes.
source: Genomic imprinting refers to the mono-allelic and parent-specific expression of a subset of genes.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that represents established scientific knowledge in the field of genomic imprinting.

claim: The paternally expressed Zdbf2 gene controls neonatal growth in mice in a dose-sensitive but parent-of-origin-independent manner.
source: Here, using mouse models of loss, gain and parental inversion of expression, we report that the paternally expressed Zdbf2 gene controls neonatal growth in mice, in a dose-sensitive but parent-of-origin-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple mouse models (loss, gain, and parental inversion) presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Zdbf2-KO neonates failed to fully activate hypothalamic circuits that stimulate appetite.
source: We further found that Zdbf2-KO neonates failed to fully activate hypothalamic circuits that stimulate appetite, and suffered milk deprivation and diminished circulating Insulin Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing downregulation of Npy and Agrp genes, and by stomach weight measurements indicating reduced milk intake.

claim: Zdbf2-KO neonates suffered milk deprivation.
source: We further found that Zdbf2-KO neonates failed to fully activate hypothalamic circuits that stimulate appetite, and suffered milk deprivation and diminished circulating Insulin Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1).
evidence: This is supported by stomach weight measurements showing reduced stomach mass relative to body mass in Zdbf2-KO pups at 3dpp.

claim: Zdbf2-KO neonates had diminished circulating Insulin Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1).
source: We further found that Zdbf2-KO neonates failed to fully activate hypothalamic circuits that stimulate appetite, and suffered milk deprivation and diminished circulating Insulin Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1).
evidence: This is supported by LUMINEX ELISA assay measurements showing reduced plasma IGF-1 levels at 1, 5, and 15 days post-partum.

claim: Only half of Zdbf2-KO pups survived the first days after birth.
source: Consequently, only half of Zdbf2-KO pups survived the first days after birth and those surviving were smaller.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curves showing approximately 56% of Zdbf2-KO males and 52% of Zdbf2-KO females alive at 3dpp.

claim: Zdbf2-KO pups that survived were smaller than wild-type littermates.
source: Consequently, only half of Zdbf2-KO pups survived the first days after birth and those surviving were smaller.
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements showing Zdbf2-KO mice were 20% lighter than WT littermates at 15dpp.

claim: Genomic imprinting arises from sex-specific patterning of DNA methylation during gametogenesis.
source: In mammals, genomic imprinting arises from sex-specific patterning of DNA methylation during gametogenesis, which generates thousands of germline differentially methylated regions (gDMRs) between the oocyte and the spermatozoa.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the mechanism of genomic imprinting.

claim: After fertilization, the vast majority of gDMRs are lost during epigenetic reprogramming.
source: After fertilization, the vast majority of gDMRs are lost during the epigenetic reprogramming that the embryonic genome undergoes (Seah and Messerschmidt, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Seah and Messerschmidt, 2018.

claim: Some gDMRs are protected through sequence- and DNA methylation-specific recruitment of the KRAB-associated protein 1 (KAP1) complex.
source: However, some gDMRs are protected through sequence- and DNA methylation-specific recruitment of the KRAB-associated protein 1 (KAP1) complex (Li et al., 2008; Quenneville et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2019) and become fixed as imprinting control regions (ICRs).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2008; Quenneville et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2019.

claim: Roughly 20 ICRs maintain parent-specific DNA methylation throughout life and across all tissues in mouse and human genomes.
source: Roughly 20 ICRs maintain parent-specific DNA methylation throughout life and across all tissues in mouse and human genomes, and control the mono-allelic and parent-of-origin expression of approximately 150 imprinted genes (Schulz et al., 2008; Tucci et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schulz et al., 2008 and Tucci et al., 2019.

claim: ICRs control the mono-allelic and parent-of-origin expression of approximately 150 imprinted genes.
source: Roughly 20 ICRs maintain parent-specific DNA methylation throughout life and across all tissues in mouse and human genomes, and control the mono-allelic and parent-of-origin expression of approximately 150 imprinted genes (Schulz et al., 2008; Tucci et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schulz et al., 2008 and Tucci et al., 2019.

claim: All life-long ICRs have probably been discovered.
source: DNA methylation-based genome-wide screens have led to the conclusion that all life-long ICRs have probably been discovered (Proudhon et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Proudhon et al., 2012 and Xie et al., 2012.

claim: Imprinted genes have long-recognized roles in development and viability in utero by balancing growth and resource exchanges between the placenta and the fetus.
source: Imprinted genes have long-recognized roles in development and viability in utero, by balancing growth and resource exchanges between the placenta and the fetus.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field of genomic imprinting.

claim: Imprinted genes strongly influence postnatal physiology.
source: Moreover, it is increasingly clear that imprinted genes also strongly influence postnatal physiology (Peters, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peters, 2014.

claim: Neonatal growth, feeding behavior, metabolic rate, and body temperature are affected by improper dosage of imprinted genes in mouse models and human imprinting disorders.
source: Neonatal growth, feeding behavior, metabolic rate, and body temperature are affected by improper dosage of imprinted genes in mouse models and human imprinting disorders (Charalambous et al., 2014; Ferrón et al., 2011; Leighton et al., 1995; Li et al., 1999; Plagge et al., 2004; Nicholls et al., 1989; Buiting, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Imprinting-related postnatal effects are recurrently linked to dysfunction of the hypothalamus.
source: Imprinting-related postnatal effects are recurrently linked to dysfunction of the hypothalamus (Ivanova and Kelsey, 2011), a key organ for orchestrating whole body homeostasis through a complex network of nuclei that produce and deliver neuropeptides to distinct targets, including the pituitary gland that in turn secretes endocrine hormones such as the growth hormone (GH).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ivanova and Kelsey, 2011.

claim: The hypothalamus appears as a privileged site for imprinted gene expression.
source: Accordingly, the hypothalamus appears as a privileged site for imprinted gene expression (Gregg et al., 2010; Higgs et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gregg et al., 2010 and Higgs et al., 2021.

claim: PWS children present neurological and behavioral impairments in particular related to feeding, in the context of hypothalamic neuron anomalies.
source: PWS children present neurological and behavioral impairments in particular related to feeding, in the context of hypothalamic neuron anomalies (Swaab, 1997; Cassidy and Driscoll, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Swaab, 1997 and Cassidy and Driscoll, 2009.

claim: Single inactivation of the PWS-associated Magel2 gene results in neonatal growth retardation, reduced food intake and altered metabolism in mouse models.
source: In mouse models, single inactivation of the PWS-associated Magel2 gene results in neonatal growth retardation, reduced food intake and altered metabolism (Bischof et al., 2007; Kozlov et al., 2007; Schaller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bischof et al., 2007; Kozlov et al., 2007; Schaller et al., 2010.

claim: Zdbf2 is a paternally expressed gene with preferential expression in the brain.
source: Zdbf2 (DBF-type zinc finger- containing protein 2) is a paternally expressed gene with preferential expression in the brain (Kobayashi et al., 2009; Greenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 2009 and Greenberg et al., 2017.

claim: Zdbf2 is one of the last-discovered genes with life-long and tissue-wide imprinted methylation.
source: It is one of the last-discovered genes with life-long and tissue-wide imprinted methylation, and conserved imprinting in mice and humans, however its function is not yet resolved (Kobayashi et al., 2009; Duffié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 2009 and Duffié et al., 2014.

claim: Zdbf2 imprinting is conserved in mice and humans.
source: It is one of the last-discovered genes with life-long and tissue-wide imprinted methylation, and conserved imprinting in mice and humans, however its function is not yet resolved (Kobayashi et al., 2009; Duffié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 2009 and Duffié et al., 2014.

claim: The Zdbf2 locus is controlled by a maternally methylated gDMR during the first week of embryogenesis.
source: We previously characterized the complex parental regulation of the Zdbf2 locus: it is controlled by a maternally methylated gDMR during the first week of embryogenesis, but for the rest of life, it harbors a somatic DMR (sDMR) that is paternally methylated (Proudhon et al., 2012; Duffié et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Proudhon et al., 2012 and Duffié et al., 2014, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: For the rest of life after the first week of embryogenesis, the Zdbf2 locus harbors a somatic DMR (sDMR) that is paternally methylated.
source: We previously characterized the complex parental regulation of the Zdbf2 locus: it is controlled by a maternally methylated gDMR during the first week of embryogenesis, but for the rest of life, it harbors a somatic DMR (sDMR) that is paternally methylated (Proudhon et al., 2012; Duffié et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Proudhon et al., 2012 and Duffié et al., 2014, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The maternal gDMR coincides with a promoter that drives paternal-specific expression of a Long isoform of Zdbf2 (Liz) transcript.
source: The maternal gDMR coincides with a promoter that drives paternal-specific expression of a Long isoform of Zdbf2 (Liz) transcript.
evidence: This is based on previous characterization of the Zdbf2 locus by the authors.

claim: In the pluripotent embryo, Liz transcription triggers in cis DNA methylation at the sDMR.
source: In the pluripotent embryo, Liz transcription triggers in cis DNA methylation at the sDMR, allowing de-repression of the canonical promoter of Zdbf2, located ~10 kb downstream (Greenberg et al., 2017; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Greenberg et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Liz is dispensable for embryogenesis itself.
source: In fact, although specifically expressed in the embryo where it undergoes stringent multi-layered transcriptional control (Greenberg et al., 2019), Liz is dispensable for embryogenesis itself.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Greenberg et al., 2019.

claim: Liz's sole function seems to epigenetically program expression of Zdbf2 later in life.
source: Its sole function seems to epigenetically program expression of Zdbf2 later in life: genetic loss-of-function of Liz (Liz-LOF) prevents methylation of the sDMR, giving rise to mice that cannot activate Zdbf2–despite an intact genetic sequence–in the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland and display reduced postnatal growth (Greenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Greenberg et al., 2017 and represents an inference from the observed phenotype.

claim: Genetic loss-of-function of Liz (Liz-LOF) prevents methylation of the sDMR.
source: Its sole function seems to epigenetically program expression of Zdbf2 later in life: genetic loss-of-function of Liz (Liz-LOF) prevents methylation of the sDMR, giving rise to mice that cannot activate Zdbf2–despite an intact genetic sequence–in the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland and display reduced postnatal growth (Greenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Greenberg et al., 2017.

claim: Liz-LOF mice cannot activate Zdbf2 in the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland despite an intact genetic sequence.
source: Its sole function seems to epigenetically program expression of Zdbf2 later in life: genetic loss-of-function of Liz (Liz-LOF) prevents methylation of the sDMR, giving rise to mice that cannot activate Zdbf2–despite an intact genetic sequence–in the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland and display reduced postnatal growth (Greenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Greenberg et al., 2017.

claim: Liz-LOF mice display reduced postnatal growth.
source: Its sole function seems to epigenetically program expression of Zdbf2 later in life: genetic loss-of-function of Liz (Liz-LOF) prevents methylation of the sDMR, giving rise to mice that cannot activate Zdbf2–despite an intact genetic sequence–in the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland and display reduced postnatal growth (Greenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Greenberg et al., 2017.

claim: Zdbf2 is expressed in various brain tissues at 2 weeks of age.
source: Using this same Zdbf2-LacZ reporter line, we confirmed the expression of Zdbf2 in various brain tissues at 2 weeks of age, and more specifically, the high specificity in hypothalamic cells that belonged to the peri- and paraventricular nuclei in the anterior area (Figure 1B), and the arcuate, the dorsomedial and the ventromedial nuclei in the lateral hypothalamic area (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Zdbf2 is highly specifically expressed in hypothalamic cells that belonged to the peri- and paraventricular nuclei in the anterior area.
source: Using this same Zdbf2-LacZ reporter line, we confirmed the expression of Zdbf2 in various brain tissues at 2 weeks of age, and more specifically, the high specificity in hypothalamic cells that belonged to the peri- and paraventricular nuclei in the anterior area (Figure 1B), and the arcuate, the dorsomedial and the ventromedial nuclei in the lateral hypothalamic area (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Zdbf2 is highly specifically expressed in the arcuate, the dorsomedial and the ventromedial nuclei in the lateral hypothalamic area.
source: Using this same Zdbf2-LacZ reporter line, we confirmed the expression of Zdbf2 in various brain tissues at 2 weeks of age, and more specifically, the high specificity in hypothalamic cells that belonged to the peri- and paraventricular nuclei in the anterior area (Figure 1B), and the arcuate, the dorsomedial and the ventromedial nuclei in the lateral hypothalamic area (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Zdbf2 expression is specific to neuronal cells and absent from non-neuronal cells of the hypothalamus.
source: Analysis of publicly available single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data further defined Zdbf2 expression to be specific to neuronal cells and absent from non-neuronal cells of the hypothalamus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of scRNA-seq data from Chen et al., 2017, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The three hypothalamic clusters where Zdbf2 was the most highly expressed were both glutamatergic (Glu13 and Glu15) and GABAergic (GABA17) neurons from the arcuate and the periventricular hypothalamic regions.
source: The three hypothalamic clusters where Zdbf2 was the most highly expressed were both glutamatergic (Glu13 and Glu15) and GABAergic (GABA17) neurons from the arcuate and the periventricular hypothalamic regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Zdbf2 is expressed in the anterior and intermediate lobes of the pituitary gland.
source: When we examined the pituitary gland by X-gal staining, we found Zdbf2 to be expressed in the anterior and intermediate lobes of the gland and almost undetectable signal in the posterior lobe (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), a pattern that was confirmed from available scRNA-seq data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; Cheung et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and scRNA-seq data from Cheung et al., 2018.

claim: Zdbf2 is almost undetectable in the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland.
source: When we examined the pituitary gland by X-gal staining, we found Zdbf2 to be expressed in the anterior and intermediate lobes of the gland and almost undetectable signal in the posterior lobe (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), a pattern that was confirmed from available scRNA-seq data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; Cheung et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Steady-state levels of Zdbf2 transcripts progressively rose in the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland after birth, reached their maximum at 2–3 weeks and then stabilized at later ages, in both males and females.
source: Finally, we further found that steady-state levels of Zdbf2 transcripts progressively rose in the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland after birth, reached their maximum at 2–3 weeks and then stabilized at later ages, in both males and females (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: At birth, Zdbf2-KO animals were present at expected sex and Mendelian ratios.
source: At birth, we found that Zdbf2-KO animals were present at expected sex and Mendelian ratios (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: There was no difference in body mass prior to birth (E18.5) between Zdbf2-KO and WT animals.
source: However, while there was no difference in body mass prior to birth (E18.5), Zdbf2-KO neonates of both sexes appeared smaller than WT littermates already at 1 and 5 days of postnatal life (day post-partum, dpp) (Figure 2B–C), indicating slower growth in the first days after birth.
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figures 2B-C.

claim: Zdbf2-KO neonates of both sexes appeared smaller than WT littermates already at 1 and 5 days of postnatal life.
source: However, while there was no difference in body mass prior to birth (E18.5), Zdbf2-KO neonates of both sexes appeared smaller than WT littermates already at 1 and 5 days of postnatal life (day post-partum, dpp) (Figure 2B–C), indicating slower growth in the first days after birth.
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figures 2B-C.

claim: At 15dpp, Zdbf2-KO mice were 20% lighter than their WT littermates.
source: At 15dpp, Zdbf2-KO mice were 20% lighter than their WT littermates (Figure 2B and E–F).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figures 2B and 2E-F.

claim: Lower body mass persisted into adulthood in Zdbf2-KO mice, measured up to 12 weeks of age.
source: Lower body mass persisted into adulthood, measured up to 12 weeks of age (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: When present on the maternal allele, the Zdbf2-∆exon six deletion had no discernable growth effect.
source: As predicted, when present on the maternal allele, the Zdbf2-∆exon six deletion had no discernable growth effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The reduced body weight phenotype in Zdbf2-KO mice was highly penetrant.
source: The reduced body weight phenotype was highly penetrant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and was not obviously due to a developmental delay: Zdbf2-KO pups and their WT littermates synchronously acquired typical hallmarks of postnatal development (skin pigmentation, hair appearance and eye opening) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
evidence: This is supported by body mass distribution data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The reduced body weight phenotype in Zdbf2-KO mice was not obviously due to a developmental delay.
source: The reduced body weight phenotype was highly penetrant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and was not obviously due to a developmental delay: Zdbf2-KO pups and their WT littermates synchronously acquired typical hallmarks of postnatal development (skin pigmentation, hair appearance and eye opening) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
evidence: This is supported by data on developmental hallmarks shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I.

claim: Zdbf2-KO pups and their WT littermates synchronously acquired typical hallmarks of postnatal development (skin pigmentation, hair appearance and eye opening).
source: The reduced body weight phenotype was highly penetrant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and was not obviously due to a developmental delay: Zdbf2-KO pups and their WT littermates synchronously acquired typical hallmarks of postnatal development (skin pigmentation, hair appearance and eye opening) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I.

claim: The growth phenotype in Zdbf2-KO mice appeared to be systemic, affecting both the body length and mass.
source: The growth phenotype appeared to be systemic: it affected both the body length and mass of Zdbf2-KO animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and a range of organs uniformly (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Adult Zdbf2-KO males exhibit an overall body mass reduction.
source: While we confirmed that adult Zdbf2-KO males exhibit an overall body mass reduction (Figure 2G), we did not observe difference in the composition of fat and bone tissues (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: This is supported by DEXA scan data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There was no difference in the composition of fat and bone tissues in adult Zdbf2-KO males compared to WT.
source: While we confirmed that adult Zdbf2-KO males exhibit an overall body mass reduction (Figure 2G), we did not observe difference in the composition of fat and bone tissues (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: This is supported by DEXA scan data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: Zdbf2-KO mice had decreased lean mass.
source: However, Zdbf2-KO mice had decreased lean mass (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by DEXA scan data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Zdbf2-KO animals exhibit the same growth defect as Liz-LOF mice, with identical postnatal onset and severity.
source: In conclusion, Zdbf2-KO animals exhibit the same growth defect that we previously reported in Liz-LOF mice, with identical postnatal onset and severity (Greenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from Zdbf2-KO and Liz-LOF mice, with citation to Greenberg et al., 2017.

claim: The regulatory landscape of the paternal allele of Zdbf2 was intact in Zdbf2-KO mice.
source: However, contrary to the Liz-LOF mice, the regulatory landscape of the paternal allele of Zdbf2 was intact in Zdbf2-KO mice: DNA methylation of the sDMR located upstream of Zdbf2 was normal, and accordingly, Zdbf2 transcription was activated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F-G).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F-G.

claim: DNA methylation of the sDMR located upstream of Zdbf2 was normal in Zdbf2-KO mice.
source: However, contrary to the Liz-LOF mice, the regulatory landscape of the paternal allele of Zdbf2 was intact in Zdbf2-KO mice: DNA methylation of the sDMR located upstream of Zdbf2 was normal, and accordingly, Zdbf2 transcription was activated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F-G).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Zdbf2 transcription was activated in Zdbf2-KO mice.
source: However, contrary to the Liz-LOF mice, the regulatory landscape of the paternal allele of Zdbf2 was intact in Zdbf2-KO mice: DNA methylation of the sDMR located upstream of Zdbf2 was normal, and accordingly, Zdbf2 transcription was activated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F-G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: A genetic mutation of Zdbf2 (Zdbf2-KO) and a failure to epigenetically program Zdbf2 expression (Liz-LOF) are phenotypically indistinguishable.
source: We therefore show that a genetic mutation of Zdbf2 (Zdbf2-KO) and a failure to epigenetically program Zdbf2 expression (Liz-LOF) are phenotypically indistinguishable.
evidence: This is based on comparison of phenotypic data from both mouse models.

claim: Liz-LOF mice show a complete lack of Zdbf2 expression.
source: As Liz-LOF mice show a complete lack of Zdbf2 expression (Greenberg et al., 2017), this incidentally supports that Zdbf2-KO mice carry a null Zdbf2 allele.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Greenberg et al., 2017.

claim: Zdbf2-KO mice carry a null Zdbf2 allele.
source: As Liz-LOF mice show a complete lack of Zdbf2 expression (Greenberg et al., 2017), this incidentally supports that Zdbf2-KO mice carry a null Zdbf2 allele.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic similarity between Zdbf2-KO and Liz-LOF mice.

claim: Although there was no Mendelian bias at 1dpp, a strong bias was apparent at 20dpp in Zdbf2-KO cohorts.
source: Indeed, analysis of Zdbf2-KO cohorts revealed that although there was no Mendelian bias at 1dpp (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), a strong bias was apparent at 20dpp: 75 WT and 44 Zdbf2-KO animals were weaned among n = 27 litters, while a 50/50 ratio was expected.
evidence: This is supported by genotype ratio data at different time points.

claim: 75 WT and 44 Zdbf2-KO animals were weaned among n = 27 litters, while a 50/50 ratio was expected.
source: Indeed, analysis of Zdbf2-KO cohorts revealed that although there was no Mendelian bias at 1dpp (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), a strong bias was apparent at 20dpp: 75 WT and 44 Zdbf2-KO animals were weaned among n = 27 litters, while a 50/50 ratio was expected.
evidence: This is direct observational data from the study.

claim: Postnatal viability was the most strongly impaired within the first days after birth in Zdbf2-KO mice.
source: Postnatal viability was the most strongly impaired within the first days after birth, with only 56% of Zdbf2-KO males and 52% of Zdbf2-KO females still alive at 3dpp, compared to 84% and 88% of WT survival at this age (Figure 2J and Figure 2—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curve data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Only 56% of Zdbf2-KO males and 52% of Zdbf2-KO females were still alive at 3dpp, compared to 84% and 88% of WT survival at this age.
source: Postnatal viability was the most strongly impaired within the first days after birth, with only 56% of Zdbf2-KO males and 52% of Zdbf2-KO females still alive at 3dpp, compared to 84% and 88% of WT survival at this age (Figure 2J and Figure 2—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curve data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: A partial postnatal lethality phenotype was also present in Liz-LOF mutants.
source: Importantly, a partial postnatal lethality phenotype was also present in Liz-LOF mutants who are equally growth-restricted as a result of Zdbf2 deficiency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H and Figure 2—source data 1B), but did not occur when the mutation was transmitted from the silent maternal allele harboring either the Zdbf2 deletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and Figure 2—source data 1C) or the Liz deletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J and Figure 2—source data 1D).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Partial postnatal lethality did not occur when the mutation was transmitted from the silent maternal allele harboring either the Zdbf2 deletion or the Liz deletion.
source: Importantly, a partial postnatal lethality phenotype was also present in Liz-LOF mutants who are equally growth-restricted as a result of Zdbf2 deficiency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H and Figure 2—source data 1B), but did not occur when the mutation was transmitted from the silent maternal allele harboring either the Zdbf2 deletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and Figure 2—source data 1C) or the Liz deletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J and Figure 2—source data 1D).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-J.

claim: When placed in an environment without WT littermates, Zdbf2-KO pups gained normal viability.
source: However, when placed in an environment without WT littermates, Zdbf2-KO pups gained normal viability (Figure 2K and Figure 2—source data 1E).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Zdbf2-KO pups are mechanically able to ingest milk.
source: Incidentally, this shows that Zdbf2-KO pups are mechanically able to ingest milk.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Zdbf2-KO pups survive normally when not competing with WT littermates.

claim: Postnatal body growth is exquisitely sensitive to the quantity of Zdbf2 produced in the hypothalamo-pituitary axis.
source: By relying on a unique collection of mouse models of total loss of function (Zdbf2-KO and Liz-LOF), partial loss of function (Zdbf2-lacZ), normal function (Zdbf2-WT), and gain of function (Zdbf2-GOF), we observed that postnatal body growth is exquisitely sensitive to the quantity of Zdbf2 produced in the hypothalamo-pituitary axis.
evidence: This is supported by data from multiple mouse models showing dose-dependent effects on body weight.

claim: Zdbf2 meets the criteria of a bona fide growth-promoting gene: growth is reduced upon decreased dosage and oppositely enhanced upon increased dosage of Zdbf2.
source: Incidentally, Zdbf2 meets the criteria of a bona fide growth-promoting gene: growth is reduced upon decreased dosage and oppositely enhanced upon increased dosage of Zdbf2 (Efstratiadis, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by data from loss-of-function and gain-of-function models, with citation to Efstratiadis, 1998.

claim: Growth reduction was more pronounced than overgrowth upon changes in Zdbf2 expression (18% decrease and 10% increase at 10dpp).
source: Consistent with previous results for the imprinted Cdkn1c gene (Andrews et al., 2007), growth reduction was more pronounced than overgrowth upon changes in Zdbf2 expression (18% decrease and 10% increase at 10dpp) and specific to males.
evidence: This is supported by body weight data from Zdbf2-KO and Zdbf2-GOF mice, with citation to Andrews et al., 2007.

claim: The Zdbf2 growth phenotype was specific to males.
source: Consistent with previous results for the imprinted Cdkn1c gene (Andrews et al., 2007), growth reduction was more pronounced than overgrowth upon changes in Zdbf2 expression (18% decrease and 10% increase at 10dpp) and specific to males.
evidence: This is supported by body weight data showing significant effects primarily in males.

claim: Bi-allelic and increased Zdbf2 expression exacerbates postnatal body weight gain in Zdbf2-GOF animals.
source: With the Zdbf2-GOF model, we were able to evaluate the consequences of a loss of Zdbf2 imprinting: bi-allelic and increased Zdbf2 expression exacerbates postnatal body weight gain.
evidence: This is supported by body weight data from Zdbf2-GOF mice.

claim: Despite being slightly bigger, viability, fertility or longevity appeared overall normal in Zdbf2-GOF animals.

evidence: This is based on comparison with published data on GH-deficient mice, with citations to Voss and Rosenfeld, 1992 and Lupu et al., 2001.

source: In Zdbf2-KO mutants, the growth defect is apparent as soon as 1dpp, as well as decreased IGF-1.

source: Our findings support that limited food intake is probably the primary defect in Zdbf2 deficiency, leading to IGF-I insufficiency in the critical period of postnatal development and consequently, growth restriction.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including reduced stomach weight, downregulation of feeding-related genes, and decreased IGF-1.

evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data at 1dpp and stomach weight measurements at 3dpp.

claim: ZDBF2 activates specialized hypothalamic neurons that motivate neonates to actively demand food (milk) from the mother right at birth, promoting the transition to oral feeding after a period of passive food supply in utero.
source: Given our observations, we propose that ZDBF2 activates specialized hypothalamic neurons that motivate neonates to actively demand food (milk) from the mother right at birth, promoting the transition to oral feeding after a period of passive food supply in utero.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the integration of multiple experimental findings.

claim: Zdbf2 is a paternally expressed gene that potentiates resource extraction from the mother, in line with the kindship theory of genomic imprinting.
source: Our results are also in line with the kindship theory of genomic imprinting (Haig, 2000): Zdbf2 is a paternally expressed gene that potentiates resource extraction from the mother.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of evolutionary theory, with citation to Haig, 2000.

claim: Decreasing Zdbf2 compromises resource acquisition and body weight gain right after birth.
source: In conclusion, we reveal here that decreasing Zdbf2 compromises resource acquisition and body weight gain right after birth.

claim: Zdbf2-KO mice do present a post-puberal spurt of growth, which attenuates their smaller body phenotype.
source: Zdbf2-KO mice do present a post-puberal spurt of growth, which attenuates their smaller body phenotype, but we never observed excessive weight gain, even after 18 months (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate calculations and long-term observations.
